egbBEA_d9Ps.visual_thesis: A side-by-side comparison of self-tickling (no reaction) versus external tickling (extreme reaction), followed by a brain-mapping visual showing the cerebellum's predictive filter.
egbBEA_d9Ps.script: You dig your fingers into your ribs, but feel nothing. Yet, if someone else barely grazes your side, you scream. Your brain is actually censoring you. Your cerebellum predicts your own touch and mutes it instantly. But it’s not just to stop a laugh. Without this sensory filter, your own clothes would feel like constant, agonizing tickling. Which is why...

uuu-mK2UTXA.title: Why You Think Red Cars Are Faster
uuu-mK2UTXA.topic: Why drivers in red cars feel faster to you
uuu-mK2UTXA.visual_thesis: Red cars appear to move faster than they actually do due to visual bias, making them seem closer and more immediate.
uuu-mK2UTXA.script: You just saw that red car fly by. But your eyes lied. Red objects demand more attention. They feel closer, more immediate. This visual bias makes red cars seem faster than they actually are. So that driver wasn't racing. Your brain just made it seem like they were.

iW2e-D5tYSs.script: You press your knife into a fresh onion. Suddenly, your eyes sting and the air feels heavy. It’s not just a strong smell. You’ve actually triggered a microscopic landmine.
